title: A pipeline of qualifications and one strategic partner
body:
## No Names on the Board

The disclosure sits in the risk factor section of POET's FY2025 20-F filing with the matter-of-fact plainness that only a securities lawyer can sustain: no major customers, no named partners, no disclosed design wins. For investors accustomed to parsing the customer-concentration tables that connectivity-silicon companies like Applied Optoelectronics or Credo Technology routinely file — tables that, for better or worse, tell you who is actually buying the product — POET's equivalent section offered structural silence. The company was qualifying with customers, it said. It was engaged in conversations. It was, in the language of photonics procurement cycles, somewhere inside the 18-to-36-month tunnel between first engineering engagement and volume purchase order.

That silence was not, by itself, alarming. It was the expected disclosure posture for a pre-commercial platform company at POET's stage. The optical interposer had been demonstrated, wafer-level integration in Singapore was operational, and management had spent the better part of 2024 and 2025 presenting the architecture at hyperscaler engineering reviews. None of that produces a named customer until it produces a design win. The FY2025 filing, honest about the gap between activity and contract, was therefore a faithful portrait of the commercial position as of December 31, 2025: a pipeline, not a revenue base.

## The Qualification Topology

POET's go-to-market architecture at the snapshot date was structured around two access points into hyperscaler procurement: the OEM/ODM channel and the direct hyperscaler engineering team. The OEM/ODM channel — names including Supermicro, Dell, HPE, and Foxconn's FII manufacturing subsidiary — represents the conventional path for optical component suppliers seeking datacenter volume. Hyperscalers increasingly design their own rack architectures and then require OEM partners to source and qualify the components that fill them. A design win at Supermicro for a hyperscaler rack programme is, in practice, a design win inside Microsoft's or Meta's infrastructure supply chain, even if the hyperscaler's name never appears on the purchase order.

The direct hyperscaler engineering path is harder and slower but more durable. Microsoft, Amazon Web Services, Meta, and Google each maintain internal silicon and photonics engineering teams that evaluate candidate architectures against internal roadmaps years ahead of procurement. A position inside those roadmaps — even a non-binding evaluation position — provides architectural leverage that can survive OEM transitions.

The critical constraint in either channel is time. Pluggable transceiver design cycles have historically run 12 to 18 months from platform engagement through volume shipment. Novel photonic-integration architectures, particularly those requiring changes to the socket, the thermal envelope, or the board power delivery — as co-packaged optics does — run longer. Industry practitioners have cited 18-to-36-month cycles as the working estimate for CPO component qualification, and some programs have exceeded that range. POET, which entered meaningful hyperscaler engagement no earlier than 2023 and scaled its Singapore fabrication line through 2024, was at the snapshot date positioned no earlier than mid-cycle in the fastest plausible programmes.

The investment implication is direct: design-in disclosure events, not quarterly revenue, are the leading indicator that the qualification cycle is closing. The absence of those disclosures in the FY2025 20-F was consistent with the timeline; it was not evidence of failure. But it left POET's commercial position as a probability distribution rather than a realised outcome.

## The One Disclosed Partner

Against the anonymity of the broader qualification pipeline, the Sivers Semiconductors collaboration announced in September 2025 stood out as the most concrete disclosed strategic relationship POET carried into the snapshot date. The partnership paired POET's Optical Interposer with custom high-power indium phosphide DFB lasers designed by Sivers Photonics, Sivers' UK subsidiary, to produce External Light Source module candidates for hyperscaler CPO supply chains.

The architecture the collaboration addressed has become one of the more contested sub-questions inside the broader CPO debate. Co-packaged optics eliminates the pluggable transceiver cage at the front panel of the switch, moving the optical engine adjacent to or inside the switch package. That migration, however, creates a laser placement problem: laser chips generate heat and have reliability lifetimes that are difficult to manage inside the thermal envelope of a tightly packaged switch ASIC. The External Light Source architecture resolves this by placing the laser module outside the switch package — still close, but thermally separated — and coupling light into the co-packaged optical engine via a short optical path.

POET's interposer-based integration platform was well-suited to ELS construction. The wafer-level assembly process that defines the Optical Interposer allows laser chips, modulators, photodetectors, and wavelength-division components to be assembled onto a passive substrate with controlled optical coupling losses. Sivers' high-power InP DFB lasers provided the light source the interposer platform needed to complete the module. The combination, according to the collaboration's framing, offered a component candidate that neither company could field independently.

What the Sivers partnership did not provide, however, was revenue, a named end customer, or a committed supply chain. Sivers Semiconductors was itself a pre-commercial photonics platform company — Stockholm-listed, with meaningful R&D investment and a credible technology base, but no volume optical production programmes at the scale hyperscaler CPO would eventually require. Two pre-commercial companies agreeing to develop a module candidate for an emerging market that had not yet placed volume orders was a statement of strategic alignment, not commercial validation. The disclosure was real and meaningful; it was not a proxy for a design win.

## Manufacturing Geography and Geopolitical Exposure

POET Singapore Pte. Ltd. operated the company's wafer-level photonic integration fabrication line at the snapshot date. Singapore's semiconductor manufacturing cluster — anchored by GlobalFoundries, Micron, and a constellation of advanced packaging facilities — provided POET with access to process equipment, materials supply, and engineering talent that would have been difficult to replicate in a smaller geography. The Singapore location also provided partial insulation from US-China trade friction, which had disrupted several competitors' supply chains in the 2023-2025 period.

The FY2025 20-F disclosed additional operations in China and Malaysia, which it listed as a geopolitical risk factor. The specific nature of those operations — whether they represented R&D functions, engineering support, or supply chain relationships — was not disclosed with enough granularity to assess the exposure precisely. OSAT (outsourced semiconductor assembly and test) relationships and specific fab partnerships were similarly not named in public filings at the snapshot date.

## The Competitive Perimeter

The qualification pipeline POET was pursuing did not exist in isolation. At the platform layer, Intel's Silicon Photonics organisation represented the most established internal-integration competitor, with the advantage of being able to co-design photonic components with Intel's switching and networking silicon. Marvell's accumulation of PAM-DSP IP through its Inphi acquisition and subsequent optical engine investments gave it a position in the CPO optical engine layer that POET would need to displace or complement.

The most consequential single competitor and demand-side validator, however, was Broadcom. The Tomahawk 5 CPO programme — Broadcom's actively shipping co-packaged optics-enabled switch ASIC at the snapshot date — simultaneously validated that hyperscaler CPO demand was real and established Broadcom as the incumbent optical-engine integrator in the programmes most likely to scale first. A hyperscaler that had already qualified a Broadcom CPO platform had less near-term procurement urgency for alternative interposer architectures, whatever their theoretical efficiency advantages.

Ayar Labs, Lightmatter, and Celestial AI represented the venture-funded wing of the competitive set — each pursuing CPO or photonic interconnect from a different architectural direction, each well-capitalised through 2024 and 2025 fundraising rounds, and none yet at volume production. The competitive field was, in short, crowded with well-funded pre-revenue companies and at least one incumbent already shipping product.

The architectural alternative scenario — in which pluggable optics continues to dominate datacenter interconnect through 2027 or beyond — pointed in a different direction entirely. If hyperscalers concluded that 400G and 800G pluggable transceivers, extended through a 1.6T generation, could satisfy AI cluster bandwidth requirements without the power density gains that CPO promised, the primary beneficiary would be Applied Optoelectronics and similar vertically integrated transceiver suppliers — not POET.

## The Ledger as It Stands

At the snapshot date, POET's customer-and-partner map was a pipeline with one disclosed anchor. The Sivers collaboration was real, technically coherent, and strategically sensible; the hyperscaler qualification activity was credible given the company's engineering investments and Singapore manufacturing capability; the 18-to-36-month cycle timing was consistent with the absence of named design wins in the FY2025 filing.

What sophisticated investors required from that position — and what the next 12-to-24 months of disclosure would either deliver or withhold — was evidence of pipeline conversion. A named OEM design-in, a disclosed hyperscaler engineering programme, or a commercial supply agreement with a CPO optical engine assembler would each represent a qualitative threshold that the FY2025 filing did not cross. The $313.4M cash position bought the time for those disclosures to arrive. It did not guarantee them. The investment proposition remained, as it had been since the $250M institutional raise closed, a binary wager on whether the Optical Interposer's qualification pipeline would crystallise into a revenue line before the architectural debate resolved against it.
